title: The hymn that asks who knows
word: the whole five years in seven sits
hookLine: a hymn of creation that ends: he surely knows, or perhaps he does not
carry: in the Veda, asking is part of faith
tomorrow: after the last class, what does an old teacher tell his students?

cards: Ask your phone where everything came from and it answers in half a second, sounding sure. The Rig Veda has a hymn about where everything came from too, and it does something odd at the end.
It names the one who watches over the world from the highest heaven, and then it says: he surely knows. Or perhaps he does not know. A creation hymn that ends on a maybe.
Why would anyone keep that in scripture?

teach.b: It's called the Nasadiya, after its opening words: there was not non-being, and not being, then. No air, no sky beyond it. Darkness hidden in darkness.
Then desire arose, the first seed of mind, and sages searching their hearts found the tie between what is and what is not. Then the questions start.
Who really knows? Who can say where this creation came from? The gods came later than its making, so who knows where it arose?

teach.h: OR PERHAPS HE DOES NOT KNOW.
teach.b: And then the ending you heard: the one who oversees it surely knows, or perhaps he does not. Here's the solve. The hymn isn't losing its nerve.

It sings its questions on purpose, inside the Rig Veda itself. Readers hear it in more than one way: honest humility before something too large, or a hint that the source is beyond any knower's words.
And here's the teaching, a big one in Hinduism: asking belongs inside faith. The questions aren't kept outside the scripture; they're sung in it.
Centuries later, the Brahma Sutras open with the same move: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman.

Years four and five on this path, the goddess, Shiva, the schools of thought set side by side, the Vedas read slowly, kept doing what this hymn does: asking out loud, from inside the tradition, and keeping the question.

how: The Nasadiya hymn (Rig Veda 10.129) is recited in Vedic chanting and read by students of the Vedas; teachers often bring it up as the Veda's own example of honest questioning.

games.q: what does “the whole five years in seven sits” mean?
o: a look back at the whole path, one sit at a time
a practice of sitting still for five years
seven long retreats spread across five years

games.q: inside the hymn. tap the pairs.

s: the Rig Veda's creation hymn says plainly that there is no god
it names the one who oversees creation and asks whether even he knows. a question, not a denial.
in the Nasadiya, the gods come after the world's making
so, the hymn asks, who could know where it arose?
the hymn opens with a god speaking the world into being
it opens before being and non-being, in darkness hidden in darkness.

games.q: a friend says a scripture that admits 'perhaps he does not know' must be unsure of itself. what does the hymn's own shape suggest?
o: that it was copied wrong by a later scribe.
that questions are sung on purpose, inside the Veda.
that the Veda gave up on the question.
games.why: the hymn asks and keeps asking, inside the Rig Veda itself. readers hear humility, or a source beyond words; the hymn doesn't settle it.

practice: Close your eyes, or lower them, and let it be dark for a while, the hymn's darkness before anything. Let one question rest there, where did all this come from, and don't reach for an answer.
When thoughts arrive, let them go back into the dark.

wordCard.voice: The whole five years in seven sits: years four and five held in one hymn that asks who really knows, and keeps asking.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Nasadiya, named for its opening words, 'there was not non-being' (na asat).

carryVoice: For the road: in the Veda, asking is part of faith. Who really knows is a question worth keeping, and the summit keeps going.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.129 (the Nasadiya Sukta: neither non-being nor being; darkness hidden by darkness; desire, the first seed of mind; the sages found the bond of being in non-being; who really knows; the gods are later; he who oversees it in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps he does not know)
Brahma Sutra 1.1.1 (athato brahma jijnasa: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman)
